objectives: Find the true subject past interrupters for agreement
Attach modifiers to the correct noun; keep series parallel

slides.title: Part 1 — Free points, if you know the rules
slides.body: Standard English Conventions (~26% of Reading & Writing) is the *most rule-bound* part of the SAT. Unlike reading, every answer is provably correct. Memorize one short rule set and these become automatic, fast points.

slides.title: The rule families tested (the complete list)
slides.body:
Every Conventions question is one of:

- **Boundaries** — sentence vs fragment vs run-on; comma splices; semicolon/colon/dash; punctuation pairing around supplements (non-essential elements take *matching* punctuation, two commas or two dashes).
- **Subject–Verb agreement** — verb number must match the *true* subject.
- **Pronoun agreement & clarity** — pronoun matches its antecedent in number; no ambiguous antecedent.
- **Verbs** — tense consistency and correct form.
- **Modifiers** — a modifier attaches to the nearest noun; opening modifiers must be followed by what they describe.
- **Parallelism** — items in a series/comparison share grammatical form.

That's it. There is no infinite well of grammar — it's this list.

slides.title: The single most tested idea: independent clauses
slides.body:
> An **independent clause** is a complete sentence (subject + verb, can stand alone). Two independent clauses **cannot** be joined by only a comma (comma splice) and **cannot** be fused with nothing (run-on).

Valid joins of two independent clauses: (1) period, (2) semicolon, (3) comma **+** a FANBOYS coordinating conjunction (*for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so*), (4) colon/dash when the second elaborates the first. A large fraction of Boundaries questions reduces to one test: *is each side independent?* If yes → strong punctuation required, a lone comma is wrong. Master this one idea and you've answered most of the domain.

slides.title: Part 2 — Strategy a top scorer uses
Find the TRUE subject; delete the interrupter
slides.body: The SAT hides the subject behind prepositional phrases and clauses: *"The **box** of rare antique coins ___ heavy."* Subject = *box* (singular), not *coins*. Procedure: mentally delete everything between the subject and the verb ("of rare antique coins"), then check agreement on what remains. Common interrupters: *of …, along with …, as well as …, including …* — none of these change the subject's number. This single deletion move resolves nearly every agreement item.

slides.title: Pronouns: name the antecedent out loud
slides.body: For every pronoun ask: *"stands for **what**, and is that thing singular or plural?"* Indefinite singulars trip people: *each, every, either, neither, anyone* are **singular** ("each of the players *was*"). And the SAT's strict rule: a pronoun with *no single clear antecedent* is **wrong even if it sounds fine** — ambiguity is an error, not a style preference.

slides.title: Modifiers: who is doing the action?
slides.body: An opening modifier attaches to the noun **immediately after the comma**. *"Walking to school, the rain soaked Maria."* — grammatically the *rain* is walking (a dangling modifier). The fix puts the real actor right there: *"Walking to school, Maria was soaked by the rain."* Whenever a sentence starts with an *-ing*/*-ed* phrase or an infinitive, immediately check: is the thing right after the comma what that phrase actually describes?

slides.title: Part 3 — Worked examples, end to end
Worked example 1 — a Boundaries item
slides.body:
*"The experiment failed three times ___ the team refused to give up."* Choices: (A) `,` (B) `;` (C) `, and` (D) ` and`.

Step 1 — independence test: "The experiment failed three times" ✓ independent; "the team refused to give up" ✓ independent. Two independents.

slides.title: Worked example 1 — walking it
slides.body:
- (A) bare comma → **comma splice** ✗.
- (D) ` and` with no comma → **run-on** (fused) ✗.
- (B) semicolon → valid join of two independents ✓.
- (C) comma + coordinating *and* → also valid ✓.

When a real item offers exactly one of {semicolon, comma+FANBOYS}, that's the answer; here the standard credited form is **(C)**. The decision was 100% mechanical — *two independents → period/semicolon/comma+FANBOYS* — no ear required.

question.question: "The data, along with the lab notes, ___ inconclusive." Correct verb:
options: was (subject = 'data' treated singular here; 'along with…' is an interrupter)
question.explanation: 'along with the lab notes' is a non-essential interrupter, not part of the subject. Delete it: 'The data … was inconclusive.' Subject–verb agreement ignores interrupters.

slides.title: Worked example 2 — agreement with an interrupter
slides.body: *"The collection of essays, which spans three decades, ___ widely praised."* Delete the interrupters *of essays* and *which spans three decades* → *"The collection ___ widely praised."* Subject = *collection* (singular) → *was*. Every distractor (*were/have been*) is generated by agreeing with *essays* or *decades* — exactly the nouns the deletion rule tells you to ignore.

slides.title: The Conventions trap families
slides.body:
1. **Ear-based comma** — a comma placed because 'a pause sounds right' between two independents (comma splice).
2. **Interrupter agreement** — verb made to agree with a noun inside the interrupting phrase, not the true subject.
3. **Dangling modifier** — the noun after the comma isn't the doer of the opening phrase.
4. **Broken parallelism** — a series mixing forms (*gerund, gerund, infinitive*).

All four are *rule* errors with provable right answers — never decide by sound.

question.question: Diagnose the mistake.
question.scenario: A student chooses a comma to join two full sentences because 'a pause sounds right there.' Wrong.

rubricCriteria.description: identifies the comma splice (two independent clauses joined by only a comma)
states the valid joins: period / semicolon / comma + FANBOYS
notes 'sounds like a pause' is not a grammar rule — test clause independence

question.explanation: Punctuation on the SAT is rule-based, not ear-based. Two independent clauses require strong punctuation; a comma alone is the textbook comma-splice trap.

hints: Who actually did the action in the opening phrase?
The noun right after the comma must be the doer.
slides.workedSolution: An introductory participial phrase modifies the noun directly after the comma. 'Working…, the report' makes the report work — dangling. Recasting so 'Dana' follows the modifier (and Dana does the verb) is the only grammatically correct option.

question.question: "___ to finish early, the report was submitted by Dana before noon." Best opening?
options: Having worked through lunch, Dana submitted the report before noon
Working through lunch, the report was finished by Dana
To finish early, the report was submitted by Dana
Finished early, the report was submitted
question.explanation: The introductory modifier must attach to the person who acted. Only the choice where 'Dana' immediately follows the modifier avoids the dangling modifier.

question.question: Parallelism requires that items in a list:
question.explanation: Series/comparisons must be parallel in form (e.g., all gerunds, all infinitives). Length/order/verb-count are irrelevant.

question.prompt: Teach back: how do you decide, in one check, whether two clauses can be joined by a comma?

rubricCriteria.description: test whether each side is an independent clause (a complete sentence)
if both are independent, a lone comma is wrong (comma splice)
valid joins: period, semicolon, or comma + a FANBOYS conjunction

question.question: State the subject–verb-agreement procedure when an interrupter is present, in your own words.

rubricCriteria.description: identify the true subject (head noun), not nouns inside interrupters
match the verb's number to the true subject

slides.title: How it scores & what's next
slides.body: Standard English Conventions is the most learnable points on the SAT — the rule set is finite and the answers provable. That completes the Reading & Writing half. Next: the **Math** domains, where the same 'method, not vibes' discipline applies and you add step-by-step derivations.
